claim: Thirty individuals (12 men, age: M = 23.0 years, SD = 4.2; education: M = 15.3 years, SD = 3.2; all right-handed) watched movie clips from The Grand Budapest Hotel while undergoing fMRI.
source: Thirty individuals (12 men, age: M = 23.0 years, SD = 4.2; education: M = 15.3 years, SD = 3.2; all right-handed) watched movie clips from The Grand Budapest Hotel while undergoing fMRI.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant demographics and experimental procedure in the manuscript.

claim: None of the participants reported previously seeing The Grand Budapest Hotel movie.
source: None of the participants reported previously seeing this movie.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant characteristics based on self-report.

claim: Participants watched a continuous 90 s clip from the movie in its original temporal order six times.
source: We analyzed data from the Intact condition, during which participants watched a continuous 90 s clip from the movie in its original temporal order. This clip was watched six times, interspersed with other video clips that are not considered here.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design and stimulus presentation.

claim: The 90 s Intact clip depicts an interview scene between the protagonist and his future employer inside of the Grand Budapest Hotel.
source: This Intact clip depicts an interview scene between the protagonist and his future employer inside of the Grand Budapest Hotel.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus content.

claim: Data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner with a 64-channel head/neck coil using a multiband echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence with repetition time = 1.5 s, echo time = 39 ms, flip angle = 50°, acceleration factor = 4, shift = 3, and voxel size = 2.0 mm iso.
source: Data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner with a 64-channel head/neck coil using a multiband echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence (repetition time = 1.5 s; echo time = 39 ms; flip angle = 50°; acceleration factor = 4; shift = 3; voxel size = 2.0 mm iso).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: T1-weighted structural images (whole-brain high-resolution; 1.0 mm iso) were acquired with an MPRAGE sequence.
source: T1-weighted structural images (whole-brain high-resolution; 1.0 mm iso) were acquired with an MPRAGE sequence.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structural imaging acquisition.

claim: Field maps (40 oblique axial slices; 3 mm iso) were collected to aid registration.
source: Field maps (40 oblique axial slices; 3 mm iso) were collected to aid registration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the field map acquisition and its purpose.

claim: The fMRI scan took place over three experimental runs, each of which contained two presentations of the Intact movie clip.
source: The fMRI scan took place over three experimental runs, each of which contained two presentations of the Intact movie clip (as well as other movie clips not considered here).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design structure.

claim: The first three EPI volumes of each run were discarded to allow for T1 equilibration.
source: The first three EPI volumes of each run were discarded to allow for T1 equilibration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the preprocessing procedure and its rationale.

claim: Data preprocessing was carried out in FSL, and included brain extraction, motion correction, high-pass filtering (max period = 140 s), spatial smoothing (3 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel), and registration to standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.
source: Data preprocessing was carried out in FSL, and included brain extraction, motion correction, high-pass filtering (max period = 140 s), spatial smoothing (3 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel), and registration to standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.
evidence: This is a direct description of the preprocessing pipeline and parameters.

claim: Each voxel's timecourse was z-scored to have zero mean and unit variance.
source: Finally, each voxel's timecourse was z-scored to have zero mean and unit variance.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the normalization procedure applied to the data.

claim: Fourteen individuals (nine men) were asked to mark event boundaries corresponding to the same 90 s Intact clip from The Grand Budapest Hotel.
source: Fourteen individuals (nine men) were asked to mark event boundaries corresponding to the same 90 s Intact clip from The Grand Budapest Hotel as shown to the fMRI participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavioral annotation task and participants.

claim: No participant reported watching the clip more than three times during the event annotation task.
source: No participant reported watching the clip more than three times.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant behavior during the annotation task.

claim: The HMM assumes that events are a sequence of discrete states.
source: This HMM assumes that (1) events are a sequence of discrete states, (2) each event is represented in the brain by a unique spatial activity pattern, and (3) all viewings of the movie evoke the same sequence of activity patterns in the same order (though possibly with different timings).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the assumptions of the HMM model used in the analysis.

claim: The HMM assumes that each event is represented in the brain by a unique spatial activity pattern.
source: This HMM assumes that (1) events are a sequence of discrete states, (2) each event is represented in the brain by a unique spatial activity pattern, and (3) all viewings of the movie evoke the same sequence of activity patterns in the same order (though possibly with different timings).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the assumptions of the HMM model.

claim: The HMM assumes that all viewings of the movie evoke the same sequence of activity patterns in the same order (though possibly with different timings).
source: This HMM assumes that (1) events are a sequence of discrete states, (2) each event is represented in the brain by a unique spatial activity pattern, and (3) all viewings of the movie evoke the same sequence of activity patterns in the same order (though possibly with different timings).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the assumptions of the HMM model.

claim: The HMM was fit with seven events to match the approximate timescale of the semantic events in the narrative.
source: The model was fit with seven events; this number was chosen to match the approximate timescale of the semantic events in the narrative, matching the mean number of events annotated by human observers (mean = 6.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model parameter choice and its justification based on behavioral data.

claim: The mean number of events annotated by human observers was 6.5.
source: The model was fit with seven events; this number was chosen to match the approximate timescale of the semantic events in the narrative, matching the mean number of events annotated by human observers (mean = 6.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavioral annotation results.

claim: Spherical searchlights had a radius of 5 voxels and were spaced with a stride of 5 voxels.
source: We generated spherical searchlights spaced evenly throughout the MNI volume (radius = 5 voxels; stride = 5 voxels).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the searchlight analysis parameters.

claim: Only searchlights with at least 20 voxels inside a standard MNI brain mask and for which at least 15 participants had valid data for all viewings were retained.
source: We retained only the searchlights with at least 20 voxels which were inside a standard MNI brain mask and for which at least 15 participants had valid data for all viewings.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inclusion criteria for searchlights in the analysis.

claim: The shared response model (SRM) was used to functionally hyperalign all participants into shared 10-dimensional space.
source: We then used the SRM (Chen et al., 2015) to functionally hyperalign all participants into shared 10-dimensional space (jointly fitting the alignment across all six viewings) and averaged their responses together.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the hyperalignment method used, with citation to the original method.

claim: The SRM hyperalignment was jointly fit across all six viewings.
source: We then used the SRM (Chen et al., 2015) to functionally hyperalign all participants into shared 10-dimensional space (jointly fitting the alignment across all six viewings) and averaged their responses together.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the hyperalignment was performed.

claim: The SRM hyperalignment produced a 10 feature by 60 timepoint data matrix for each of the six viewings.
source: This produced a 10 feature by 60 timepoint data matrix for each of the six viewings, which was input to the HMM analysis described above.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dimensionality of the data after hyperalignment.

claim: Statistical significance was assessed using a permutation-based null hypothesis testing approach with 100 permutations (1 real + 99 null).
source: To assess statistical significance, we utilized a permutation-based null hypothesis testing approach. We constructed null datasets by randomly shuffling each participant's six responses to the six presentations of the movie clip. The full analysis pipeline (including hyperalignment) was run 100 times, once on the real (unpermuted) dataset and 99 times on null (permuted) datasets, with each analysis producing a map of anticipation across all voxels.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical testing procedure.

claim: Voxels were determined significant at q<0.05 after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction.
source: Voxels were determined significant (q<0.05) after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, as implemented in AFNI (Cox, 1996).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical threshold and correction method used.

claim: Multiple regions exhibited shifts in event timing between initial and repeated viewings, with event transitions shifting earlier in time with subsequent viewings.
source: Multiple regions exhibited shifts in event timing between initial and repeated viewings, with event transitions shifting earlier in time with subsequent viewings.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2a showing the brain regions with anticipatory shifts.

claim: Anticipation timescales varied from a few seconds to 15 s across the brain.
source: Across the brain, anticipation timescales varied from a few seconds to 15 s, with the longest timescale anticipatory signals in prefrontal cortex and the temporal pole.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by the color scale in Figure 2a.

claim: The longest timescale anticipatory signals were found in prefrontal cortex and the temporal pole.
source: Across the brain, anticipation timescales varied from a few seconds to 15 s, with the longest timescale anticipatory signals in prefrontal cortex and the temporal pole.
evidence: This claim is directly stated and can be observed in Figure 2a showing yellow regions in these areas.

claim: Anticipation followed a posterior-to-anterior hierarchy, with progressively anterior areas generating anticipatory signals that reach further into the future (Spearman's rho = 0.58, p=0.0030).
source: Anticipation followed a posterior-to-anterior hierarchy, with progressively anterior areas generating anticipatory signals that reach further into the future (Spearman's rho = 0.58, p=0.0030).
evidence: This claim is directly stated with statistical support and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: The magnitude of temporal shift varied along a posterior-to-anterior temporal hierarchy (Spearman's rho = 0.58, p=0.0030).
source: The magnitude of this shift varied along a posterior-to-anterior temporal hierarchy (Spearman's rho = 0.58, p=0.0030), with the most anterior regions in the temporal pole and prefrontal cortex showing shifts of up to 15 s on subsequent viewings compared to the first viewing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the main finding with statistical support.

claim: The most anterior regions in the temporal pole and prefrontal cortex showed shifts of up to 15 s on subsequent viewings compared to the first viewing.
source: The magnitude of this shift varied along a posterior-to-anterior temporal hierarchy (Spearman's rho = 0.58, p=0.0030), with the most anterior regions in the temporal pole and prefrontal cortex showing shifts of up to 15 s on subsequent viewings compared to the first viewing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the maximum anticipation observed in specific brain regions.

claim: The posterior-to-anterior hierarchy of anticipation persisted in the unthresholded anticipation map (Spearman's rho = 0.42, p=0.0028).
source: This hierarchy persisted even when computed on the unthresholded anticipation map including voxels that did not meet the threshold for statistical significance (Spearman's rho = 0.42, p=0.0028; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a supplementary analysis with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant correlations between anticipation and the left-to-right axis (rho = 0.06, p=0.41 for thresholded map; rho = 0.12, p=0.29 for unthresholded map).
source: There were no significant correlations with the left-to-right axis (rho = 0.06, p=0.41 for thresholded map; rho = 0.12, p=0.29 for unthresholded map) or the inferior-to-superior axis (rho = 0.07, p=0.28 for thresholded map; rho = −0.11, p=0.73 for unthresholded map).
evidence: This is a direct statement about null findings with statistical support.

claim: There were no significant correlations between anticipation and the inferior-to-superior axis (rho = 0.07, p=0.28 for thresholded map; rho = −0.11, p=0.73 for unthresholded map).
source: There were no significant correlations with the left-to-right axis (rho = 0.06, p=0.41 for thresholded map; rho = 0.12, p=0.29 for unthresholded map) or the inferior-to-superior axis (rho = 0.07, p=0.28 for thresholded map; rho = −0.11, p=0.73 for unthresholded map).
evidence: This is a direct statement about null findings with statistical support.

claim: A similar anticipation map was obtained when comparing the first viewing to just the sixth viewing alone.
source: We obtained a similar map when comparing the first viewing to just the sixth viewing alone (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a supplementary analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Regions with longer intrinsic timescales showed a greater degree of anticipation with repeated viewing.
source: Regions with longer intrinsic timescales also showed a greater degree of anticipation with repeated viewing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relationship between intrinsic timescales and anticipation, supported by a figure.

claim: Anticipation is further reaching in regions with longer timescales (Spearman's rho = 0.319, p=0.00031).
source: Anticipation is further reaching in regions with longer timescales (Spearman's rho = 0.319, p=0.00031).
evidence: This claim is directly stated with statistical support in the figure caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A simple cross-correlation approach detected significant anticipation in some anterior regions but was much less sensitive than the HMM fits, especially in posterior regions.
source: We also compared these results to those obtained by using a simple cross-correlation approach, testing for a fixed temporal offset between the responses to initial and repeated viewing. This approach did detect significant anticipation in some anterior regions, but was much less sensitive than the more flexible HMM fits, especially in posterior regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of two analysis methods with reference to a figure showing the results.

claim: Three clusters in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG), fusiform gyrus (FG), and superior temporal sulcus (STS) showed optimal lag for repeated viewings that was significantly earlier than for the initial viewing.
source: We found three clusters in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG), fusiform gyrus (FG), and superior temporal sulcus (STS) in which the optimal lag for the repeated viewings was significantly earlier than for the initial viewing, indicating that the relationship between the brain-derived HMM event boundaries and the human-annotated boundaries was changing with repeated viewings (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings with reference to a figure.

claim: The HMM boundaries on the first viewing were significantly later than the annotated boundaries in FG and STS.
source: The HMM boundaries on the first viewing were significantly later than the annotated boundaries in FG and STS, while the optimal lag did not significantly differ from 0 in MTG (95% confidence intervals for the optimal lag, in seconds: MTG = [−0.27, 2.86]; FG = [0.14, 1.99]; STS = [1.48, 8.53]).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing relationship with statistical support via confidence intervals.

claim: The optimal lag for MTG on first viewing did not significantly differ from 0 (95% confidence interval: [−0.27, 2.86] seconds).
source: The HMM boundaries on the first viewing were significantly later than the annotated boundaries in FG and STS, while the optimal lag did not significantly differ from 0 in MTG (95% confidence intervals for the optimal lag, in seconds: MTG = [−0.27, 2.86]; FG = [0.14, 1.99]; STS = [1.48, 8.53]).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical result with confidence interval.

claim: The HMM boundaries on repeated viewings were significantly earlier than the annotated boundaries in all three regions (MTG, FG, and STS).
source: The HMM boundaries on repeated viewings were significantly earlier than the annotated boundaries in all three regions (95% confidence intervals for the average optimal lag, in seconds: MTG = [−4.06, –1.83]; FG = [−1.56, –0.26]; STS = [−3.06, –1.69]).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing relationship with statistical support via confidence intervals.

claim: With repeated viewing, the brain's event boundaries came to precede human-annotated boundaries by 1–4 s on average.
source: With repeated viewing, the brain's event boundaries came to precede human-annotated boundaries by 1–4 s on average.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main finding about the shift in event boundary timing.

claim: Learning about temporal structure is adaptive because it enables the generation of expectations.
source: Learning about temporal structure is adaptive because it enables the generation of expectations.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the theoretical motivation for the study.

claim: A primary function of the brain is to adaptively use past experience to generate expectations about events that are likely to occur in the future.
source: A primary function of the brain is to adaptively use past experience to generate expectations about events that are likely to occur in the future (Clark, 2013; Friston, 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about brain function supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Anticipation and prediction are ubiquitous in the brain, spanning systems that support sensation, action, memory, motivation, and language.
source: Indeed, anticipation and prediction are ubiquitous in the brain, spanning systems that support sensation, action, memory, motivation, and language (den Ouden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the widespread nature of anticipation in the brain, supported by a citation.

claim: The visual system takes advantage of the world's relative stability over space and time to anticipate upcoming input.
source: For example, the visual system takes advantage of the world's relative stability over space and time to anticipate upcoming input (de Lange et al., 2018; Summerfield and Egner, 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about visual system function supported by citations.

claim: The majority of studies examining anticipatory signals have tested anticipation based on memory for relatively simple associations between pairs of discrete stimuli.
source: The majority of studies examining anticipatory signals, however, have tested anticipation based on memory for relatively simple associations between pairs of discrete stimuli, such as auditory tones, lines, dots, oriented gratings, or abstract objects (e.g., Alink et al., 2010; Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Hindy et al., 2016; Kok et al., 2012; Kok et al., 2014; Kok and Turk-Browne, 2018).
evidence: This is a direct characterization of prior research with multiple citations.

claim: Previous studies have found anticipatory signals about a single upcoming stimulus in a variety of brain regions, from perceptual regions to the medial temporal lobe.
source: These studies have found anticipatory signals about a single upcoming stimulus in a variety of brain regions, from perceptual regions (Kok et al., 2012) to the medial temporal lobe (Hindy et al., 2016; Kok and Turk-Browne, 2018).
evidence: This is a direct summary of prior findings with citations.

claim: The brain integrates information about the recent past over a hierarchy of timescales.
source: Prior work has shown that the brain integrates information about the recent past over a hierarchy of timescales (Aly et al., 2018; Hasson et al., 2015; Kurby and Zacks, 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: Lower-order areas primarily represent the current moment, whereas higher-order areas are sensitive to information from many seconds or even minutes into the past.
source: Lower-order areas primarily represent the current moment, whereas higher-order areas are sensitive to information from many seconds or even minutes into the past.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temporal hierarchy in the brain based on prior work.

claim: Higher-order regions with longer timescales play a critical role in organizing perceptual input into semantically meaningful schematic representations.
source: Higher-order regions with longer timescales play a critical role in organizing perceptual input into semantically meaningful schematic representations (Baldassano et al., 2017; Baldassano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of higher-order regions with citations.

claim: Higher-order regions exhibited anticipatory signals when individuals had prior knowledge of the general structure of a narrative.
source: We previously found that higher-order regions did exhibit anticipatory signals when individuals had prior knowledge of the general structure of a narrative (Baldassano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement about prior findings from the authors' previous work.

claim: The bilateral anterior insula has been linked to anticipation of diverse categories of positive and negative outcomes.
source: One region showing long-timescale anticipatory signals was the bilateral anterior insula. This region has been linked to anticipation of diverse categories of positive and negative outcomes (Liu et al., 2011), including outcomes that will be experienced by other people (Singer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of the anterior insula with citations.

claim: The anterior insula has been linked to anticipation of outcomes that will be experienced by other people.
source: This region has been linked to anticipation of diverse categories of positive and negative outcomes (Liu et al., 2011), including outcomes that will be experienced by other people (Singer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of the anterior insula with a citation.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) tracks high-level narrative schemas.
source: Other regions showing long timescales of anticipation include the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), which tracks high-level narrative schemas (Baldassano et al., 2018) and has been proposed to play a general role in event prediction (Alexander and Brown, 2014), and lateral prefrontal cortex, including the inferior frontal gyrus, which processes structured sequences across multiple domains (Uddén and Bahlmann, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about mPFC function with a citation.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex has been proposed to play a general role in event prediction.
source: Other regions showing long timescales of anticipation include the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), which tracks high-level narrative schemas (Baldassano et al., 2018) and has been proposed to play a general role in event prediction (Alexander and Brown, 2014), and lateral prefrontal cortex, including the inferior frontal gyrus, which processes structured sequences across multiple domains (Uddén and Bahlmann, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a proposed function of mPFC with a citation.

claim: The inferior frontal gyrus processes structured sequences across multiple domains.
source: Other regions showing long timescales of anticipation include the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), which tracks high-level narrative schemas (Baldassano et al., 2018) and has been proposed to play a general role in event prediction (Alexander and Brown, 2014), and lateral prefrontal cortex, including the inferior frontal gyrus, which processes structured sequences across multiple domains (Uddén and Bahlmann, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of the inferior frontal gyrus with a citation.

claim: Lateral occipital and ventral temporal cortex exhibit event-specific patterns during recall.
source: We also observed shorter-timescale anticipation throughout lateral occipital and ventral temporal cortex, which, though primarily thought to process bottom-up visual information, also exhibits event-specific patterns during recall (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of these regions with a citation.

claim: A top-down memory-driven signal could be responsible for driving anticipatory activation in lateral occipital and ventral temporal regions during repeated movie viewing.
source: A top-down memory-driven signal could be responsible for driving anticipatory activation in these regions during repeated movie viewing (Finnie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a possible mechanism with a citation.

claim: Some prior fMRI studies have been able to observe anticipatory signals in early regions such as V1.
source: We did not observe widespread anticipatory signals in primary sensory areas, although some prior fMRI studies have been able to observe such signals in early regions such as V1 (Alink et al., 2010; Ekman et al., 2017; Hindy et al., 2016; Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: Lerner et al., 2011 demonstrated hierarchical cortical dynamics in participants who listened to variants of a 7 min narrative that was scrambled at different timescales.
source: Lerner et al., 2011 demonstrated hierarchical cortical dynamics in participants who listened to variants of a 7 min narrative that was scrambled at different timescales (e.g., paragraphs, sentences, or words).
evidence: This is a direct description of a prior study with citation.

claim: Response reliability varied based on the timescale of scrambling in the Lerner et al., 2011 study, with higher-level brain regions responding consistently to only the more-intact narrative conditions.
source: Response reliability, measured as the correlation in BOLD activity timecourses across individuals, varied based on the timescale of scrambling, with higher-level brain regions responding consistently to only the more-intact narrative conditions.
evidence: This is a direct description of findings from the Lerner et al., 2011 study.

claim: Using intracranial EEG (iEEG), Honey et al., 2012 observed progressively longer temporal receptive windows in successive stages of the cortical hierarchy in participants who watched intact and scrambled versions of the movie Dog Day Afternoon.
source: Likewise, using intracranial EEG (iEEG), Honey et al., 2012 observed progressively longer temporal receptive windows in successive stages of the cortical hierarchy in participants who watched intact and scrambled versions of the movie Dog Day Afternoon.
evidence: This is a direct description of a prior study with citation.

claim: The process memory framework describes hierarchical memory timescales that process, represent, and support longer and longer units of information.
source: These findings can be described by the process memory framework (Hasson et al., 2015), where hierarchical memory timescales process, represent, and support longer and longer units of information.
evidence: This is a direct description of a theoretical framework with citation.

claim: The current results extend the process memory framework, suggesting that the timescales in these regions are relevant not only for online processing and memory, but also for future anticipation or simulation.
source: These results extend the process memory framework, suggesting that the timescales in these regions are relevant not only for online processing and memory, but also for future anticipation or simulation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the current findings relate to and extend a theoretical framework.

claim: Most studies examining anticipation have used fixed, shorter timescales.
source: Although prior work has uncovered anticipatory and predictive coding in the brain, most studies have examined fixed, shorter timescales of anticipation.
evidence: This is a direct characterization of prior research.

claim: Shorter timescales of anticipation have often been studied using simple, non-narrative stimuli such as objects moving across the screen, short visual sequences, and visual pattern completion tasks.
source: Moreover, these shorter timescales have often been studied using simple, non-narrative stimuli such as objects moving across the screen, short visual sequences, and visual pattern completion tasks (Alink et al., 2010; Ekman et al., 2017; Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Hindy et al., 2016; Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct characterization of prior research with citations.

claim: Some studies have used dynamic movie stimuli, but anticipation was measured via correlations between initial and repeated viewing of a movie at a constant fixed lag of 2 s.
source: Some studies have used dynamic movie stimuli, but anticipation was measured via correlations between initial and repeated viewing of a movie at a constant fixed lag of 2 s (Richardson and Saxe, 2020).
evidence: This is a direct description of a prior study's methodology with citation.

claim: Elliott Wimmer and Büchel, 2019 examined single timescales up to 30 s ahead in OFC-VMPFC regions in a maze task.
source: Research investigating longer timescales of anticipation, such as learning future state representations in a maze task, examined single timescales up to 30 s ahead in OFC-VMPFC regions (Elliott Wimmer and Büchel, 2019).
evidence: This is a direct description of a prior study with citation.

claim: Kandylaki et al., 2016 demonstrated that predictive processing of referents in narratives can be modulated by voice (passive vs. active) and causality (high vs. low).
source: Some studies that use narrative stimuli have examined specially constructed texts in order to manipulate predictions about upcoming sentences; for example, work by Kandylaki et al., 2016 demonstrated that predictive processing of referents in narratives can be modulated by voice (passive vs. active) and causality (high vs. low).
evidence: This is a direct description of findings from a prior study with citation.

claim: In a naturalistic setting where structure exists at many timescales, anticipation at multiple levels can occur in parallel across different brain regions.
source: Our results show that in a naturalistic setting, in which structure exists at many timescales, anticipation at multiple levels can occur in parallel across different brain regions.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a main conclusion from the current study.

claim: The current study found anticipation up to approximately 15 s into the future with a 90 s stimulus.
source: We found anticipation up to approximately 15 s into the future with our 90 s stimulus, but future work with stimuli of longer duration could uncover even longer timescales of anticipation, on the scale of minutes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings and their limitations.

claim: Future work with stimuli of longer duration could uncover even longer timescales of anticipation, on the scale of minutes.
source: We found anticipation up to approximately 15 s into the future with our 90 s stimulus, but future work with stimuli of longer duration could uncover even longer timescales of anticipation, on the scale of minutes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about potential future findings.

claim: Simultaneously maintaining expectations at varying timescales could allow for flexible behaviors.
source: Simultaneously maintaining expectations at varying timescales could allow for flexible behaviors, because different timescales of anticipation may be helpful for a variety of tasks and actions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Taking action to avoid immediate harm or danger would require shorter timescales of prediction, whereas cultivating social relationships demands predictions on longer timescales.
source: Taking action to avoid immediate harm or danger would require shorter timescales of prediction, whereas cultivating social relationships demands predictions on longer timescales.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing examples of how different timescales of prediction might be functionally relevant.

claim: The current results are consistent with those of Baldassano et al., 2017, in which some participants listening to an audio narrative had advance knowledge of the high-level events of the story.
source: These results are consistent with those of Baldassano et al., 2017, in which some participants listening to an audio narrative had advance knowledge of the high-level events of the story (because they had previously watched a movie version of the narrative).
evidence: This is a direct comparison to prior work with citation.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2017 observed shifts in event boundaries in higher-level regions including angular gyrus, posterior medial cortex, and mPFC using a similar HMM approach.
source: Using a similar HMM approach as in this paper, the authors observed shifts in event boundaries in higher-level regions including angular gyrus, posterior medial cortex, and mPFC.
evidence: This is a direct description of findings from a prior study with citation.

claim: In the current study, participants were repeatedly exposed to an identical movie stimulus, allowing them to generate expectations at a broad range of timescales.
source: In the current study, however, participants were repeatedly exposed to an identical movie stimulus, allowing them to generate expectations at a broad range of timescales, including the timescales of fast-changing low-level visual features.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and its implications.

claim: The current approach allowed observation for the first time that anticipation occurs in both low- and high-level regions, with shorter-timescale anticipation in visual occipital regions and the furthest-reaching anticipatory signals in prefrontal cortex.
source: This novel approach allowed us to observe for the first time that anticipation occurs in both low- and high-level regions, with shorter-timescale anticipation in visual occipital regions and the furthest-reaching anticipatory signals in prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the novelty and findings of the current study.

claim: The current model detects anticipation as temporal shifts in events and assumes that the underlying event patterns themselves are constant.
source: Our model detects anticipation as temporal shifts in events, and though timepoints can reflect 'mixed' event assignments, it assumes that the underlying event patterns themselves (Figure 1b) are constant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the assumptions of the model used.

claim: The successor representation model describes a representation in which each state comes to include features of future events, weighted by their likelihood of occurring and their distance into the future.
source: One example is the 'successor representation' model from the field of reinforcement learning, which describes a representation in which each state (here, event representation) comes to include features of future events, weighted by their likelihood of occurring and their distance into the future (Dayan, 1993).
evidence: This is a direct description of a theoretical model with citation.

source: The upward shift from the first viewing to subsequent viewings indexes the amount of anticipation.

source: We found that regions throughout the brain exhibit anticipation of upcoming events in audiovisual stimuli, with activity patterns shifting earlier in time as participants repeatedly watched the same movie clip.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the advantage of the probabilistic approach.

source: We then computed the amount of anticipation as the average AUC for repeated viewing (viewings 2–6) minus the AUC for the first viewing.
evidence: This is a direct description of how anticipation was quantified.

source: We then performed a one-tailed statistical test (described below) to determine whether this difference was significantly positive, indicating earlier event transitions with repeated viewing.

source: Not only does this approach provide a way of quantifying anticipation, it gives us a trajectory of the most likely event at any given timepoint, as well as the onset and duration of each event.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the outputs of the HMM analysis.

claim: A one-tailed p-value was obtained in each voxel by fitting a normal distribution to the null anticipation values and finding the fraction of this distribution that exceeded the real result in that voxel.
source: A one-tailed p-value was obtained in each voxel by fitting a normal distribution to the null anticipation values, and then finding the fraction of this distribution that exceeded the real result in this voxel (i.e., showed more anticipation than in our unpermuted dataset).
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical testing procedure.

claim: To obtain a p-value for the correlation between Y-coordinate and anticipation, the observed correlation was compared to a null distribution in which the Spearman's correlation was computed with null anticipation values from the permutation analysis.
source: To obtain a p-value, the observed correlation was compared to a null distribution in which the Spearman's correlation was computed with the null anticipation values from the permutation analysis described above, in which the order of the viewings was randomly scrambled for each participant.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical testing procedure.

claim: The optimal number of events for each searchlight was determined by maximizing the log-likelihood of the HMM on the first movie viewing.
source: To relate the timescales of anticipation to the intrinsic timescales of brain regions during the first viewing, we fit the HMM on the first viewing alone, varying the number of events from 2 to 10. The HMM was trained on the average response from half of the participants (fitting the sequence of activity patterns for the events and the event variance) and the log-likelihood of the model was then measured on the average response in the other half of the participants. The training and testing sets were then swapped, and the log-likelihoods from both directions were averaged together. Hyperalignment was not used during this fitting process, to ensure that the training and testing sets remained independent. The number of events that yielded the largest log-likelihood was identified as the optimal number of events for that searchlight.
evidence: This is a direct description of the procedure for determining optimal number of events.

claim: Hyperalignment was not used during the fitting process for determining optimal number of events, to ensure that the training and testing sets remained independent.
source: Hyperalignment was not used during this fitting process, to ensure that the training and testing sets remained independent.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a methodological choice and its rationale.

claim: The optimal number of events was compared to the anticipation timescale in each region using Spearman's correlation.
source: The optimal number of events was then compared to the anticipation timescale in that region (from the main analysis), using Spearman's correlation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis procedure.

claim: A cross-correlation approach was used to test whether the repeated-viewing timecourse was significantly ahead of the initial-viewing timecourse.
source: For comparison, we also ran a searchlight looking for anticipatory effects using a non-HMM cross-correlation approach. Within each searchlight, we obtained an average timecourse across all voxels and correlated the response to the first viewing with the average response to repeated viewings at differing lags. Using the same quadratic-fit approach for identifying the optimal lag described below, we tested whether the repeated-viewing timecourse was significantly ahead of the initial-viewing timecourse (relative to a null distribution in which the viewing order was shuffled within each subject).
evidence: This is a direct description of a comparison analysis.

claim: Event boundary annotations were convolved with the HRF to obtain an event boundary timecourse.

evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis procedure with reference to a figure.

evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis procedure with reference to a figure.

claim: Moments with high boundary strength indicate moments in which the brain pattern was rapidly switching between event patterns.
source: Moments with high boundary strength indicate moments in which the brain pattern was rapidly switching between event patterns.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of what high boundary strength means.

claim: The HMM boundary strength timecourse for each viewing was cross-correlated with the annotated event boundary timecourse, shifting the annotated timecourse forward and backward to determine the optimal temporal offset.
source: We cross-correlated the HMM boundary strength timecourse for each viewing with the annotated event boundary timecourse, shifting the annotated timecourse forward and backward to determine the optimal temporal offset (with the highest correlation).
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis procedure.

claim: The timing of the peak correlation was measured by identifying the local maximum in correlation closest to 0 lag, then fitting a quadratic function to the maximum correlation lag and its two neighboring lags and recording the location of the peak of this quadratic fit.
source: We measured the timing of the peak correlation by identifying the local maximum in correlation closest to 0 lag, then fitting a quadratic function to the maximum correlation lag and its two neighboring lags and recording the location of the peak of this quadratic fit.
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis procedure.

source: We measured the amount of shift between the optimal lag for the first viewing and the average of the optimal lags for repeated viewings, and obtained a p-value by comparing to the null distribution over maps with permuted viewing orders (as in the main analysis), then performed an FDR correction.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical testing procedure.

claim: Three gray matter clusters were identified as significant at q<0.05 in the comparison of HMM boundaries to annotated boundaries.

claim: To assess whether the optimal lags differed from 0 in the three identified clusters, the cross-correlation analysis was repeated in 100 bootstrap samples resampling from the raters who generated the annotated event boundaries.
source: To statistically assess whether the optimal lags differed from 0 in the three searchlights maximally overlapping these three clusters, we repeated the cross-correlation analysis in 100 bootstrap samples, in which we resampled from the raters who generated the annotated event boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct description of the bootstrap analysis procedure.
